title: Competency framework vs capability framework: what is the difference?
description: Competency frameworks set assessable standards for roles; capability frameworks describe the skills, knowledge and behaviors a whole workforce needs.
shortAnswer: A competency framework defines the demonstrated performance a role requires, usually as competencies with performance standards and evidence that can be assessed. A capability framework describes the skills, knowledge and behaviors an organization or sector needs across its whole workforce, often including future-oriented and personal attributes, graded by level. The terms overlap heavily and are often used interchangeably; the practical test is whether the framework defines assessable standards and evidence.
keyTakeaways: Competency usually means demonstrated performance against a standard; capability usually means the broader ability, including behaviors and potential, that work at a given level calls for.
Public sector frameworks often use capability language: the NSW Public Sector Capability Framework sets 20 capabilities in 5 groups at 5 levels for every role in the sector.
US Department of Labor competency models define a competency as a cluster of knowledge, skills and abilities that can be measured against well-accepted standards.
Many frameworks blend both: SFIA pairs professional skills with generic attributes such as autonomy, influence and complexity at seven levels.
For regulated roles, a capability framework rarely replaces competency standards; it sits alongside them.

sections.heading: What is the core difference between a competency framework and a capability framework?

blocks.text: The core difference is emphasis. A competency framework emphasizes what a person must demonstrably do in a role, to a standard, with evidence. A capability framework emphasizes the range of skills, knowledge and behaviors the organization needs across many roles, now and in future, described at levels that work for recruitment, development and career planning.

The competency side is defined precisely in workforce systems. A US Department of Labor competency model published through the Competency Model Clearinghouse defines a competency as "a cluster of related knowledge, skills, and abilities that affects a major part of one's job (a role or responsibility), that correlates with performance on the job, that can be measured against well-accepted standards, and that can be improved via training and development" ([US Department of Labor, Electronic Health Records Competency Model](https://www.dol.gov/sites/dolgov/files/ETA/advisories/TEN/2011/ten14_11a1.pdf)). See [competency framework](/glossary/competency-framework).

The capability side is illustrated by public sector frameworks. For example, the Office of the Public Service Commissioner in New South Wales, Australia, says its [Public Sector Capability Framework](https://www.nsw.gov.au/nsw-government/public-sector-capability-framework/how-to-apply-framework) "gives a common way to describe skills, knowledge and behaviours for public sector roles", and is used for role design, recruitment, performance, learning and career planning across the sector.

sections.heading: What does a capability framework look like in practice?

blocks.text: A capability framework typically lists a fixed set of capabilities in groups, defines levels, and describes each level through behavioral indicators. The NSW Public Sector Capability Framework is a well-documented public example of this structure.

According to the Office of the Public Service Commissioner's [fact sheet on the revised framework](https://www.nsw.gov.au/nsw-government/public-sector-capability-framework/framework-guidance/factsheet-for-revised-framework) (January 2026), the framework was first published in 2013 and "retains the same 20 capabilities across 5 capability groups: Personal Attributes, Relationships, Results, Business Enablers and People Management". It has five levels (Foundational, Intermediate, Adept, Advanced and Highly Advanced), and behavioral indicators "describe the types of behaviours or actions that indicate effective performance at each capability level". The revision strengthened customer service, cultural capability, and digital and data literacy, and agencies are asked to update existing role descriptions by January 29, 2027.

The same fact sheet notes that occupation-specific capability sets (for example for finance, procurement and ICT professionals) sit alongside the core framework. That pairing is common: a sector-wide capability layer for every role, and a more technical layer for specific occupations.

sections.heading: Do some frameworks combine both approaches?

blocks.text: Yes. Many frameworks combine role-specific skills with generic, capability-style attributes, and their names do not reliably signal which emphasis they have.

items: **SFIA (Skills Framework for the Information Age)** describes professional skills alongside generic attributes, namely autonomy, influence, complexity, knowledge, and business skills and behavioral factors, across seven levels of responsibility. The [SFIA Foundation](https://sfia-online.org/en/about-sfia/how-sfia-works) states that each level "represents increasing responsibility, accountability and impact in the workplace".

**US Department of Labor competency models** are built in tiers. In the Electronic Health Records model, tiers 1 to 3 hold foundation competencies (personal effectiveness, academic and workplace competencies) that apply across industries, while tiers 4 and 5 hold industry-wide and industry-sector technical competencies. The lower tiers read much like a capability framework; the upper tiers like a technical competency standard.
**Internal frameworks** in regulated organizations often use capability language for leadership and behaviors and competency language for technical and regulatory tasks.

blocks.title: Judge by content, not by name
blocks.text: If a framework states performance criteria and the evidence an assessor must see, it is working as a competency framework whatever it is called. If it describes behaviors at levels for development and selection, it is working as a capability framework.

sections.heading: When should an organization use each?

blocks.text: Use a capability framework to describe what good looks like across the whole workforce and to support recruitment and development. Use competency standards to decide whether a person may perform a specific role or task, particularly where a regulator, auditor or licensing body will ask for evidence.

blocks.text: Both layers draw on a shared vocabulary of skills, which is where a [skills taxonomy](/glossary/skills-taxonomy) helps, and both need a [proficiency scale](/glossary/proficiency-scale) whose levels assessors can tell apart. The related comparison of [competency framework vs skills framework](/compare/competency-framework-vs-skills-framework) covers the vocabulary side.

sections.heading: How does Knowledge Foundry approach this?

blocks.text: Knowledge Foundry does not ask organizations to choose between the two. It links capabilities and competencies to the concepts, obligations and assessment points beneath them, so a behavioral capability and a technical competency can both be traced to the evidence that supports them.

faqs.q: Is capability just another word for competency?
faqs.a: Often, yes in practice. Many organizations use the words interchangeably. Where a distinction is drawn, capability tends to mean the broader ability, including behaviors and potential, while competency means demonstrated performance against a defined standard. Each framework should define its own terms.

faqs.q: Can a capability framework satisfy a regulator's competence requirement?
faqs.a: Rarely on its own. Regulators and auditors generally want evidence that people performing regulated activities are competent for those activities. Behavioral capability levels support that case but usually need role-specific competency standards and assessment records alongside them.

faqs.q: How many levels should a capability framework have?
faqs.a: Published frameworks vary. The NSW Public Sector Capability Framework uses five levels, and SFIA uses seven levels of responsibility. The right number is the smallest one whose descriptions assessors and managers can apply consistently.

faqs.q: Should capability and competency frameworks be owned by the same team?
faqs.a: They work best with a single owner of the shared vocabulary and levels, even if different teams maintain content. When HR owns capabilities and compliance owns competencies separately, the two often drift apart and roles end up with conflicting requirements.
